content: 1. Health services, goods, and facilities must be designed to respect the cultural values of individuals, minorities, and communities. They should also be sensitive to gender and life-cycle requirements, while ensuring confidentiality and improving the health status of those they serve. 2. Health facilities, goods, and services must not only be culturally acceptable but also scientifically and medically appropriate, maintaining high standards of quality. 3. Core obligations include ensuring non-discriminatory access to health facilities, goods, and services, particularly for vulnerable or marginalized groups. 4. Access to nutritionally adequate and safe food must be guaranteed to prevent hunger for all individuals. 5. Basic shelter, housing, sanitation, and a sufficient supply of safe and potable water must be accessible to everyone. 6. Essential medicines, as defined by the WHO Action Programme on Essential Drugs, must be provided to those in need. 7. Equitable distribution of all health facilities, goods, and services must be ensured. 8. The role of organizations such as WHO, the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, the International Committee of the Red Cross/Red Crescent, UNICEF, and other non-governmental organizations is critical in disaster relief and humanitarian assistance, especially during emergencies and for refugees and internally displaced persons. 9. Access to palliative care and essential medicines, including opioid analgesics like morphine, is a fundamental component of the right to the highest attainable standard of health and well-being. 10. Palliative care is an ethical responsibility of health systems, and healthcare professionals have a duty to alleviate physical, psychosocial, and spiritual pain and suffering, regardless of whether the underlying condition is curable. 11. End-of-life care is a critical component of palliative care, addressing the needs of individuals with life-limiting conditions. 12. Over 40 million people require palliative care annually, and this need is expected to grow due to aging populations and the increasing prevalence of chronic and non-communicable diseases. 13. Palliative care for children is of particular importance, and Member States should estimate the quantities of internationally controlled medicines needed, including pediatric formulations. 14. Palliative care must be integrated across the continuum of care, particularly at the primary care level, to address inequities in access to such services. 15. The availability and appropriate use of internationally controlled medicines for pain and symptom relief remain insufficient in many countries, necessitating efforts to remove regulatory barriers while preventing misuse and diversion. 16. Education and training for healthcare providers, caregivers, and community volunteers are essential to address the lack of knowledge and skills in palliative care. 17. Palliative care employs an interdisciplinary approach to meet the needs of patients and their families, and strong networks between professional providers, support care providers, volunteers, and affected families are crucial for delivering quality care. 18. Palliative care must be included in universal health coverage definitions and provided equitably to meet the needs of patients. 19. Adequate funding mechanisms for palliative care programs, including medicines and medical products, are essential, particularly in developing countries. 20. Palliative care actions and indicators should be integrated into global monitoring frameworks for non-communicable diseases and other health initiatives. 21. Medicines for pain and symptom control in palliative care settings should be included in national essential medicines lists, reflecting the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines. 22. Partnerships between governments and civil society, including patient organizations, should be fostered to support palliative care services. 23. Research on effective palliative care models, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, should be encouraged to identify best practices. 24. The WHO Director-General is urged to ensure that palliative care is integrated into global health plans, including those for non-communicable diseases and universal health coverage. 25. Evidence-based guidelines and tools for palliative care, including pain management, should be developed and disseminated. 26. National health systems should integrate palliative care across disease groups and levels of care, addressing ethical issues such as equitable access and person-centered care. 27. WHO should support Member States in reviewing and improving national legislation and policies to balance the prevention of misuse and diversion of controlled substances with appropriate access to medicines. 28. Collaboration with international organizations, such as the International Narcotics Control Board and UNICEF, is essential to promote the availability of controlled medicines for palliative care. 29. The global situation of palliative care should be monitored, and progress in initiatives and programs should be evaluated in collaboration with Member States and international partners. 30. Adequate funding and improved cooperation for palliative care programs and research initiatives, particularly in resource-poor countries, should be encouraged. 31. Palliative care and symptom relief must be integrated into responses to humanitarian emergencies and crises, ensuring that the needs of affected populations are addressed comprehensively.
